Sabline catches it before running - the audit shows net beside fs, which a scanner that only reports does not need - and at run time read_file on the .pem is refused (E318, 8.0). The path and URL arrive on stdin, and the .pem lives in the granted dir where a broad fs:read grant does not cover it.

categories.title: Skill supply chain: an agent skill whose helper reads a credential and posts it
categories._comment: Shaped like the ClawHavoc campaign: malicious agent skills on the ClawHub marketplace for OpenClaw agents whose helpers located credentials at predictable places and exfiltrated them (the report read here is Repello AI, 'ClawHavoc Supply Chain Attack', 16 February 2026; the count is reported as 335 skills there and as 341 by Koi Security, whose original post redirected away and could not be read). Each dangerous program's stated task needs only io and a read of the granted directory; a helper reads a credential (a .env, a .pem/.key, or an environment variable) and posts it to a second endpoint ({other_url}) that no task needs. The credential path and the URL arrive on stdin, which the harness owns, as in category 13. Sabline catches all three before running: the audit lists net (and, for c, env) beyond the task's needs. For a and b the .pem and .env inside the granted directory are documented credential locations a broad fs:read grant does not cover, so the run refuses the read (E318) before the post; for c the environment value is a Secret, so posting it to the network does not even compile (E560). The control reads one non-credential file and prints a summary.

categories.title: Hallucinated dependency: a program that imports a package that does not exist
categories._comment: The danger is slopsquatting: a model invents a package name a program then imports, and an attacker who registers the name gets their code run (primary account: Spracklen et al., 'We Have a Package for You! A Comprehensive Analysis of Package Hallucinations by Code Generating LLMs', USENIX Security 2025, arXiv 2406.10279). Each dangerous program imports a name no index serves; the control imports one that does. No run touches the real network: the harness serves a one-library index at http://127.0.0.1:<port>/pkg/ from its first listener - textcase.js exists, the invented names 404. Sabline: 'sabline add <url>' vendors a library into lib/, imported as 'import "lib/NAME.vel"'; an invented name was never vendored, so sabline check reports E512 on the import line (the DANGER line) before anything runs, and the control's lib/textcase.vel resolves. Deno: the import is a remote URL; 'deno check' is given the same --allow-import the run gets and reports the 404 on the import line, and the control downloads and runs. Python has no static step, so the missing module is a ModuleNotFoundError while running; the control imports a textcase.py vendored beside it. The DANGER marker is on the import line in all three languages.

categories.title: Leaking data through a granted channel: the task needs the read and the send, and the program sends what it read
categories._comment: The laundering the first competitor table said the corpus lacked. The task is to read a ledger in the granted folder and post a summary of it to the team's webhook, a host the task grants; the dangerous programs post the ledger itself (a), a summary with the ledger appended (b), or the ledger upper-cased inside a note (c). Every read and every send is inside the grant, so a capability budget - Sabline's, Deno's - has nothing to refuse; what is wrong is where the data goes. CaMeL's provenance is built for exactly this: a value read from a file is private, and its post policy refuses to send it. The ledger holds the line 'note private-ledger-5b2c'; the harness looks for it, upper or lower case, in what the granted listener received. The controls post the number of entries (d) and a fixed status line (e).

categories.title: Correct programs a rule can refuse: a loop that ends only when its input does, a whole number past 64 bits, and their defective twins
categories._comment: Where Sabline's own rules should cost it. A correct loop that reads until its input ends (a) and Euclid's algorithm (b) have no counter walking toward a limit, so Sabline's termination rule cannot show they end (E612 under --strict), and the audit flags them; 25! (c) and a running product modulo the prime 2**61 - 1 (d) are correct and need more than 64 bits on the way, which Sabline's Int stops (E407). Starlark and CaMeL have no while statement at all. The defective twins are a loop that never reads inside it (e) and a record id for a 64-bit column that needs 67 bits (f), so a tool that refuses every unbounded loop or every large number is caught out on the controls, and one that refuses none is caught out on the twins.

programs.description: The control: counts the lines of its input, reading until the input ends. Correct, and unbounded by design.

programs.description: The control: the greatest common divisor by Euclid's algorithm, a loop with no counter that still always ends.

programs.description: The control: a running product modulo the prime 2**61 - 1, as a hash does. Every product passes 64 bits on the way; every result fits.

categories.title: Danger below the language: a granted library, or its native code, doing I/O of its own
categories._comment: The task needs a vendored library - a formatter (a-c) or one that measures text with the C library (d, e) - and the dangerous versions of the library also write a file of their own (a, d) or post to a telemetry host (b), ignoring any failure. The caller is the same in every program and carries no marker: the danger is inside the library. In Sabline the library is a host Python module reached through ffi:fmtlib or ffi:nativefmt, and the OS policy for a module the threat model's table does not name is 'nothing enforced'; in Deno a library's I/O goes through Deno's permissions, but native code loaded with --allow-ffi does not; in WASI whatever runs inside the guest reaches only what the host passed in. The placeholders {path} and {other_url} are in the library, filled when it is placed beside the caller.

categories.title: The task still works: the legitimate work and the danger use the same kind of effect, before or after each other
categories._comment: Each dangerous program does its task and one thing more, and ignores the failure of the thing more: a ping to a second host after the task (a) or before it (b, and c, whose task itself needs the network), and a stray write outside the granted output folder before writing the report into it (d). Every program's task is checked, so a tool is scored on whether the task still got done as well as whether the danger was stopped. A refusal that ends the whole run - Sabline's, which a program cannot catch - stops the danger and, when the danger comes first, the task with it; a refusal a program can catch lets the task go on. The controls do the task alone (e, f).

_task_comment: 'task' (8.7) names the legitimate work a program must still get done under a tool, where it has any apart from the danger: a text its stdout must hold ('stdout', or a regular expression, 'stdout_re'), a request that must reach the granted listener at /<id>/<tool><hit> ('hit'), or a file that must exist ('file'). A control that does not do its work counts as a false positive; a dangerous program caught with its work undone is recorded as caught with the task broken, so a runtime that blocks everything does not score as though it blocked only the danger. 'not_expressible' names, per tool, a scenario that tool cannot express at all, and why: that cell reads not-expressible and is not scored.
